introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: 6. (a) Locate the Western Highlands naming THREE mountain peaks and describe the relief characteristics of the region. (9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Location (about 4 marks).** The Western Highlands lie in the west of Cameroon, in the **West and North-West Regions**, roughly between latitudes 5 and 7 degrees N and longitudes 9 and 11 degrees E. They are bounded by the coastal lowlands and the Mbo plain in the south-west, by the Nigerian border and the Cameroon-Nigeria highlands in the north-west, and by the Noun valley, the Mbam valley and the Adamawa Plateau in the east and north-east. They form part of the **Cameroon Volcanic Line**, which trends south-west to north-east from Mount Cameroon.

**Three peaks.**
- **Mount Oku** (about 3,000 m, the highest of the highlands) in the North-West Region, with a crater lake and a montane forest;
- **Mount Bamboutos** (about 2,700 m) on the border of the West and South-West Regions;
- **Mount Manengouba** (about 2,400 m) at the southern end of the highlands, with a twin-crater caldera and crater lakes.

On the outline map, shade the region and mark the three peaks with triangles, named, with a key.

**Relief characteristics (about 5 marks).**
- **High plateaux and mountains.** A series of **volcanic plateaux** at about 1,000 to 2,000 m (the Bamenda or Grassfields plateau, the Bamileke plateau and the Bamoun plateau) topped by **volcanic massifs and peaks** rising to over 2,000 m, some above 3,000 m.
- **Volcanic landforms.** Lava plateaus, cones, **calderas and crater lakes** (for example Lake Nyos and Lake Wum, and the crater lakes on Mount Manengouba) and basalt columns and waterfalls.
- **Steep scarps.** Steep escarpments and faulted edges on the south and west sides, where the highlands fall abruptly to the Mbo plain and the coastal lowlands.
- **Dissected by rivers.** Deep valleys and gorges and waterfalls (the Noun, the Mbam, the Menchum and the Metchum rivers and their tributaries) and rapids, which give a **rugged, broken landscape** with rounded hills and narrow valleys.
- **Climatic effect.** Altitude gives a cool, rainy climate and a **watershed** function: rivers flow towards the Atlantic (Wouri, Mungo, Cross River), the Benue (towards the Niger) and the Sanaga.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Use any THREE human factors to compare the nature of population distributions on the Western Highlands and the Adamawa Plateau. (9 marks)

(ii) Explain any TWO reasons why Douala and Yaounde are "primate cities" in Cameroon. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(b)(i) Population distribution: Western Highlands and Adamawa Plateau (9 marks).** The Western Highlands are **densely populated** (often more than 100 inhabitants per square kilometre, with the Bamileke plateau among the densest rural areas of the country), with a nucleated, almost continuous pattern of villages and chiefdoms. The Adamawa Plateau is **sparsely populated** (often fewer than 10 inhabitants per square kilometre) with scattered villages and small settlements concentrated on the roads and in a few towns (Ngaoundere).

| Human factor | Western Highlands | Adamawa Plateau |
|---|---|---|
| **Economic activity** | Intensive labour-demanding farming (coffee, maize, beans, vegetables, tubers), small plots, market gardening; many markets and small trade | Extensive cattle ranching and grazing on large areas (Fulani herders), which needs few people per square kilometre; farming is limited |
| **History and social organisation** | Old, well organised chiefdoms and kingdoms (Bamileke, Bamoun, Grassfields), strong family land tenure and attachment to the homeland, large families; refuge area in the past | Nineteenth-century wars and raiding, transhumance and the pastoral way of life produced a mobile and scattered population |
| **Infrastructure, towns and services** | Many market towns and administrative centres (Bafoussam, Bamenda, Dschang, Foumban), roads, schools and hospitals attract and hold people; high densities have also caused out-migration towards Douala and Yaounde | Few towns and poor roads outside the main axis; the railway reached Ngaoundere in the 1970s, but services remain fewer and the area is remote |

A conclusion: human factors explain why a high-density, nucleated population contrasts with a low-density, dispersed one.

**(b)(ii) Douala and Yaounde as primate cities (5 marks).** A **primate city** is a city that is much larger than the second city of the country and that dominates it politically, economically and culturally. Each of the two has several million inhabitants, several times more than the next cities (Garoua, Bamenda, Bafoussam, Maroua). Two reasons (any two):
1. **Functions.** Yaounde is the **political and administrative capital**: ministries, the presidency, embassies, universities and many institutions. Douala is the **economic capital and main seaport**: the port and airport, banks, head offices and most industries, and the transit gateway for Chad and the Central African Republic. These functions attract investment and employment.
2. **Concentration of services and infrastructure** (roads, airports, electricity, water, hospitals, universities) built there by the state and private firms, which draws migrants from all over the country (rural exodus), so the population keeps growing faster than that of the other towns.
3. **Historical advantage**: Douala was the colonial coastal gateway and Yaounde was made the capital, so investment was concentrated there.
